siiru.title: Siiru: one app for every step to Umrah
siiru.summary: I design Siiru, a companion app for Muslims in Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore. It brings 17 services together, from daily prayer and giving to booking a guide, a ride or travel insurance.

cover.alt: Three Siiru app screens: guide booking, home and Send Dua

sections.heading: The problem: Umrah planning is scattered
body: Around 1.7 million Muslims from Southeast Asia travel to Makkah every year. Planning a self-organised Umrah can take 40 to 60 hours across five or more vendors for visas, hotels, transport, guides and insurance, and none of them stays with the pilgrim before, during and after the trip.
Siiru wants to be the one companion that does. My job is to make seventeen services feel like one calm product.

sections.heading: Most users are not travelling this year
body: Most people who open an Umrah app are not flying soon. Their connection to Makkah is daily: prayer, giving, and sending a dua with a friend who is going. So we shaped the app around four modes instead of one booking funnel.

items: Prayer times, giving and dua for everyone
Guides, rides and worship in Makkah and Madinah
Returning the duas people carried, and giving again

blocks.text: An app people already open every day is trusted by the time they plan a trip. That is why daily features lead the home screen.

sections.heading: Eight screens and the decision behind each
body: These are recordings from the live app. Most of the flows are my designs, and I set the final visual style for all of them.

items: The next prayer and an AI travel assistant come first. Services sit one tap below.
Experience, languages, rating, wheelchair support and price are on the card, so guides can be compared at a glance.
Seats and luggage space come before price, with a certified driver badge.
Guided questions replace an empty prompt, and the AI shows the steps it takes.
Active protection, the claim deadline and three steps sit on the first screen.
Each gift is a concrete item with a price and one Donate button.
Pilgrims create a dua folder; friends add duas through a WhatsApp link.
Seventeen services grouped by intent, with New and Soon labels.

sections.heading: Making guide booking feel safe
body: Booking a mutawwif means trusting a stranger with the most important days of your year. If comparing two guides means opening two profiles, people hesitate or leave the app to ask around on WhatsApp.

I put the trust signals people ask about on the card itself and kept Quick Book there too. To test it, I prepared a think-aloud usability study that covers finding the feature, choosing a guide, scheduling and checkout, scored with the System Usability Scale.

sections.heading: Designing AI that people trust
body: Plan Your Trip turns a few answers into a complete Umrah itinerary. Two decisions shaped it. There is no empty prompt box, because most people have never planned a trip like this and do not know what to ask. And while the AI works, it shows its steps in plain words, such as finding places in Madinah and fitting prayer times, so the plan feels considered rather than generated.

sections.heading: The product film
body: I directed and built a two-minute film in Remotion, so the video is a React project. One project renders five versions, each with its own language, currency and voice-over. Prices inside the recorded app screens are found with OCR and rewritten in RM or S$, and an automated check reviews all 19 scenes in every version before export.

sections.heading: Beyond the app
body: The same principles carry into Siiru's web presence. With AI as a pair programmer, I designed and built a new company profile and a public report that shows donors where their gifts went.

sections.heading: How I work with the team
body: Every new design or iteration at Siiru goes through critique with developers, the PM and the leadership team. Critique is where competing priorities become shared decisions; the booking flow is one design that changed because of it.
I also mentor a junior designer through weekly one-on-ones, tasks aimed at specific gaps, and a monthly team checkpoint that shows each designer their progress and pace.

sections.heading: Siiru's impact so far
body: These are company figures, shared for scale. They belong to the whole team and its partners.

sections.heading: What I am learning
body: Seventeen services can easily become seventeen competing priorities. The work that matters most is deciding what each person needs right now, and hiding the rest.

siiru.part: I designed most of the app's core flows and own its final visual style and design decisions, across app and web. I also made the product film, mentor a junior designer and run design critiques.

hijra-ekyc.title: Making identity verification easier to get right
hijra-ekyc.summary: Three iterations of Hijra's ID check. Clearer capture guidance and an explicit review step moved more new customers to automatic approval instead of manual review.

cover.alt: Hijra e-KYC screens: ID capture, data review, selfie and result

sections.heading: The problem: people did not check what the OCR read
body: Hijra's low approval rate pushed registrations into manual review, creating work for operations and support, with up to 100 registration and e-KYC tickets a month.
The cause was human. People trusted the OCR result and skipped checking the details it extracted from their ID. Errors that took seconds to fix turned into days of manual review.

blocks.alt: The original Hijra e-KYC flow from introduction to ID capture and data entry
blocks.caption: The original flow: capture the ID, then a long form most people skimmed.

sections.heading: 2022: a countdown before continuing
body: The first iteration added a five-second review countdown. It tested well in moderated sessions, but in production a timer alone did not make the extracted data clearer. Slowing people down is not the same as helping them check.

blocks.alt: First iteration of the identity data review screen
blocks.caption: 2022: a review screen with a short countdown.

sections.heading: 2023: an explicit review step
body: I removed the timer, brought the personal details onto the review screen, added a confirmation sheet and clarified the ID photo frame so captures were sharper from the start.
Automated approvals rose 13%, and we received no complaints about the flow from Q2 to Q4.

blocks.alt: Second iteration with an ID frame, data review and confirmation sheet
blocks.caption: 2023: clearer frame, review, then a confirmation sheet.

sections.heading: 2024: helping people recover from errors
body: A change in the OCR service brought new errors, and regulation limited how quickly we could switch vendors. I redesigned around the constraint: capture guidance for both the ID and the selfie, field-by-field confirmation, and clear failure messages with an easy way to try again.
After three failed attempts, people are routed to manual review rather than stuck.

blocks.alt: Capture guidance for the ID photo, the selfie and the selfie with ID
blocks.caption: 2024: guided capture for the ID, the selfie and the selfie with ID.

blocks.alt: Tips screens comparing correct and incorrect ID and selfie photos
blocks.caption: Tips that show a good and a bad photo before the camera opens.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: The final iteration shipped at the end of Q4 2024. By February 2025, automated approvals were up 16%, with fewer customers waiting on manual review and less load on operations and support.

sections.heading: What I learned
body: When software does the reading, design has to make checking easy. The best fixes came from working with operations and compliance, and from being honest about what the verification service could and could not do.

hijra-ekyc.note: Results as reported in the original project study.
hijra-ekyc.part: I owned all three iterations, from capture guidance to review and recovery, working with the PM, engineers, operations and compliance.

hijra-homepage.title: A clearer homepage for everyday banking
hijra-homepage.summary: Hijra's home screen had grown crowded as teams added features and promotions. I rebuilt its hierarchy around the actions and benefits customers use most.

cover.alt: Redesigned Hijra homepage on two phones

sections.heading: The problem: every team wanted a spot
body: Over time, teams had each added a widget. Important promotions sat low on the page, oversized components took valuable space, and customers did not always understand the benefits they already had.

sections.heading: What customers told us
body: We interviewed employees and entrepreneurs aged 25 to 35 with medium to high digital confidence and balances of up to IDR 5 million. Three themes came up again and again: unclear benefits, weak prompts to act, and features people could not find.

blocks.alt: Menu exploration and proposed solutions for the Hijra homepage
blocks.caption: Menu exploration and proposed solutions.

sections.heading: Agreeing on one order
body: Cross-team ideation and four rounds of design critique, which I facilitated with people from several divisions, turned competing requests into one order: core banking actions first, then featured services, campaigns, prayer times and spiritual wellbeing.

blocks.alt: Design critique boards from the first round to the final prototype
blocks.caption: Four rounds of critique, from options to prototype.

sections.heading: Making the case for the balance section
body: My lead and several teammates disagreed with my design for the balance section. Instead of defending it on taste, I walked them through concrete reasoning and a side-by-side comparison of the expected impact of each option. The team agreed to go with my direction.

sections.heading: The design: benefits people can see
body: Essential actions stay central and relevant campaigns move up. Small motion cues, such as the free-transfer label, show value without adding clutter.

blocks.alt: The full revised Hijra homepage with grouped actions, services and campaigns
blocks.caption: The revised homepage, top to bottom. Scroll inside the frame.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: Monthly transactional users grew 12% and engagement time 8%. Follow-up feedback also showed better awareness of the benefits customers already had.

sections.heading: What I learned
body: Information hierarchy is agreed before it is laid out. When the people behind competing requests help shape the order, the result lasts beyond the next roadmap.

hijra-homepage.note: Results as reported in the original project study.
hijra-homepage.part: I reshaped the information hierarchy, designed the new homepage and facilitated four rounds of critique with people from several divisions to agree on it.

hijra-first-100k.title: Giving people a reason to join before the bank launched
hijra-first-100k.summary: While Hijra's banking features waited for regulatory approval, research led us to everyday Islamic lifestyle features that made the app useful from the first day.

sections.heading: The problem: a bank without banking, for now
body: Hijra's early product had limited banking features while approval was in progress. Research showed people had little reason to register when the features they expected were not there yet.

sections.heading: What people needed every day
body: We focused on Muslim adults aged 20 to 35, including employees, entrepreneurs and students, and used interviews to find everyday needs the app could support beyond money.

blocks.alt: Research and ideation map for Hijra's early product
blocks.caption: Research synthesis and ideation.

sections.heading: The direction: a reason to come back
body: The direction brought together daily prayers and dhikr, Islamic events and recordings, questions answered by experts, and clearer prayer times. We also improved Quran reading, including the move from Indo-Pak to Uthmani script.

sections.heading: Delivery in one quarter
body: Product, design and business development shaped the direction together. The features were built over a quarter, supported by partnerships and programmes such as the Halfdeen series.

sections.heading: Outcome
body: Hijra reached its first 100,000 users. It was a team milestone, supported by product work and partnerships, not by design alone.

sections.heading: What I learned
body: When the expected product is not ready, research can find another reason for people to come. The strongest direction matched real motivations with what the team could deliver. Some research details remain confidential.

hijra-first-100k.note: The 100K milestone is reported in the original project study and was a team achievement.
hijra-first-100k.part: I helped turn interview insights into the product direction, then designed the lifestyle features with product and business development.

pertamina-hmi.title: Making fuel depot operations easier to read
pertamina-hmi.summary: A redesign of a legacy control screen for Pertamina's Banjarmasin fuel depot, grouped around the operator's task, with animation that shows loading progress.

cover.alt: Redesigned dark control screen with a tanker loading illustration

sections.heading: The problem: status was there, but hard to read
body: The legacy interface used a dated style and scattered information. Operators had to work harder to read the status of fuel loading and to see how the controls related to each other.

blocks.alt: Original Pertamina fuel depot control screen
blocks.caption: Before: the legacy loading screen.

sections.heading: The design: grouped around the task
body: I regrouped related information, removed visual clutter and used a dark interface for clearer contrast in a control room. What operators need to understand and act on during loading comes first.

blocks.caption: After: grouped controls, clear status and calm contrast.

sections.heading: Motion that reports progress
body: The tanker illustration and loading animation make the process easy to follow at a glance. Here, motion reports system status; it is not decoration.

sections.heading: Scope and limits
body: This was a five-day brief with about twelve hours of design work. No usability results were measured, so this case shows the reasoning rather than a quantified improvement.

pertamina-hmi.part: I worked on it alone, from regrouping the information to the visual design and the loading animation.

hijra-loyalty.title: Hijra loyalty levels
hijra-loyalty.summary: An exploration of four journey levels, Hijrah, Hamasah, Istiqomah and Qudwah, that make progress in ethical banking visible.

cover.alt: Hijra loyalty level screens on two phones

sections.heading: Four levels, one journey
body: Each level explains a stage of progress in ethical banking, from Hijrah to Qudwah.

sections.heading: Always show the next step
body: The level screen separates completed milestones, the current stage and the next goal. A progress bar gives each achievement context instead of a standalone badge.

sections.heading: Celebrate, then point forward
body: An achievement screen marks a new level and shows the way to the next goal, in encouraging language rooted in the product's values.

sections.heading: Scope
body: This is an interface exploration. No research or launch evidence exists, so no business impact is claimed.

compfest-ux-academy.title: Judging the COMPFEST 16 UX Academy
compfest-ux-academy.summary: I judged the User Experience Academy at COMPFEST 16, Universitas Indonesia's annual technology festival, evaluating five teams of emerging designers.

cover.alt: Certificate for Ridwan's role as a COMPFEST UX Academy judge

sections.heading: The event
body: COMPFEST is organised every year by students of the Faculty of Computer Science at Universitas Indonesia. The 2024 User Experience Academy ran from 2 to 18 August with five teams of five participants.

sections.heading: My role
body: I evaluated the teams' work with a product lens, looking for clear problem framing, evidence and decisions, not only polish. This entry records the contribution; it does not claim a measured learning outcome.

mahabbati.title: Mahabbati: a ta'aruf app with an AI matchmaker
mahabbati.summary: Mahabbati helps Muslims find a spouse through ta'aruf, the Islamic way of getting to know someone for marriage, and then prepare for the wedding itself. Its flagship is an AI matchmaker that turns a few words about the person you hope for into ranked, verified matches.
mahabbati.part: I designed the whole app as a freelance product designer in 2026, from the AI matchmaker to verification, membership, pre-marriage learning and the wedding organizer. I also directed and built its company profile film and vertical promo.

cover.alt: Three Mahabbati app screens: the AI search, the home screen with match scores, and a candidate's compatibility

sections.heading: The problem: ta'aruf left hanging
body: Ta'aruf is meant to be calm and intentional. On many apps, a request is read and never answered, the quota it used is gone, and there is no easy way to tell whether a profile is real.
Mahabbati's own Google Play reviews and Instagram comments raised the same worries: paying for requests that go nowhere, and how to know a candidate is genuine. The design answers each of them.

sections.heading: The flagship: an AI matchmaker
body: Instead of a long filter form, people describe who they hope for in their own words, such as "patient and prays five times a day". The AI suggests criteria to refine the search and returns ranked recommendations, each with a match percentage.

On a candidate's page, the score never stands alone. It is labelled with what it means and what it is based on: verified profiles and sharia-aligned criteria. A high number invites a closer look; it does not make the decision.

items: Plain-language criteria, suggested filters and 11 ranked matches.
"You might match" cards carry the match score from the first screen.
An 89% compatibility score with its reason, before any request is sent.

sections.heading: Ta'aruf with a deadline
body: Every request has a clear deadline. If there is no reply within seven days, it is cancelled automatically and the quota comes back. The Ta'arufku screen shows how much time is left on each request, so nobody waits without knowing.

items: Incoming, sent and ongoing requests, each with the days left before it closes.
Fill in everything now, or just enough to start and finish later.

sections.heading: Trust and privacy, by design
body: Every user goes through the same check, local or international: an e-KTP for Indonesians or a passport for everyone else, plus a selfie. Women's photos are reviewed only by female admins. Candidate cards use illustrated avatars, and a real photo opens for 24 hours only after a request is accepted, without a download option.

items: International users verify with a passport, in the same flow as everyone else.
A clear summary before the details go to the admin team.

sections.heading: From introduction to walimah
body: Mahabbati keeps going after the match. Members prepare through classes and a pre-marriage exam with a certificate, keep up with daily duas and prayer times, and can book a sharia wedding organizer in the same app. Membership tiers decide how many requests and benefits each member gets.

items: A score, a certificate and the lessons to review next.
Short lessons from teachers, with an audio version.
What each tier unlocks, and how many requests are left.
Packages with what is included, down to catering and crew.

sections.heading: The films
body: To introduce the app, I directed and built an 88-second company profile in Remotion, in Indonesian, English and Arabic, which reads right to left. A 45-second vertical promo for Reels and TikTok follows a problem, agitation and solution arc taken from real reviews: a request left on read, a quota lost, then the quota coming back.

blocks.label: Mahabbati 45-second vertical promo, English edition, with captions on screen

sections.heading: Beyond the app
body: With AI as a pair programmer, I also designed and built Mahabbati's microsite for its sharia wedding organizer, with a path into the ta'aruf app for people still searching.

items: Sharia wedding organizer, from khitbah to walimah
